extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of moral philosophy; critics of Kant; general educated readers interested in ethical theory
extracted.subtask_description: Extract and summarize the evaluative standards and conceptual criteria used in a philosophical critique of Kant's moral theory (the Categorical Imperative, autonomy, dignity, ends/means, duties). Focuses on what a sound moral principle must avoid or satisfy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle must be more than an indication (not merely a 'finger-post')
rubrics_metrics.description: The formula expressing the moral law should itself be the moral law, not only a 'finger-post' or indication where the law is to be sought for (Kant's formula is only an indication).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A satisfactory ethical principle should state directly what is to be done rather than merely point to some other source or require additional hidden criteria to be interpreted. Anti-pattern: presenting a maxim that requires further private assumptions (e.g., invoking tacit egoism) before it yields obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: No tacit presupposition of egoism/reciprocity
rubrics_metrics.description: A moral precept should not tacitly presuppose that agents 'can only wish' what is to their advantage (i.e., rely on egoism or conditional reciprocity) as its justificatory criterion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware moral formulations that depend on the agent imagining themselves as 'possibly passive' and only accepting duties because they desire reciprocity (examples in Kant: refusal to wish for lying because others would not believe promises). Such hidden egoistic assumptions convert supposedly categorical rules into conditional rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categorical must not be covertly hypothetical
rubrics_metrics.description: If a purported Categorical Imperative actually requires a condition (e.g., that the universalized law also apply to what is done to me), then it is really a hypothetical imperative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test whether the law presupposes desires, contingency, or reciprocity; if so, it fails to be truly categorical. Example anti-pattern: deriving prohibition from 'would make promises impossible (people wouldn't believe me)' — that is conditional on beliefs and psychology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceptual coherence of central terms ('end in itself', 'absolute worth')
rubrics_metrics.description: Key concepts used in a moral theory must be logically coherent; phrases like 'end in itself' or 'absolute/incomparable value' that imply 'contradictio in adjecto' are unacceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require definitions that make sense without self-contradiction. 'End' is meaningful only in relation to a will; 'worth' is comparative and relative. Anti-pattern: employing grand-sounding terms to hide lack of intelligible content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral claims must not contradict observable human nature or empirical facts
rubrics_metrics.description: A moral principle that renders as 'unthinkable' phenomena that in fact exist and are commonplace (e.g., rule of might, suicide) fails as a foundation for ethics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure theory can account for or explain real human behaviour and extreme cases. Example: Kant declaring suicide 'unthinkable' as a universal law contradicts observed occurrences of suicide; classification of duties must not rely on denying actual human tendencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivation of duty-classes must be natural, not forced
rubrics_metrics.description: A credible moral system should allow a natural derivation of distinctions such as duties of law (perfect) versus duties of virtue (imperfect), rather than forcing the classification through strained arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for explanations that follow straightforwardly from the foundational principle. Anti-pattern: manufacturing contrived thought-experiments so that one class of duties becomes 'unthinkable' while another is merely 'not to be wished for'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid grounding morality on theological or metaphysical sleights-of-hand
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral foundations should not covertly smuggle in theological assumptions (e.g., 'absolute ought', 'end in itself', or 'pure reason practical') when these cannot be conceived or empirically grounded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demand reasons that do not rely on positing unobservable, unprovable entities or capacities. If a notion cannot be conceived or shown to exist, it lacks credentials to support moral obligation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value/dignity must be intelligible and comparative, not absolute nonsense
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that human dignity is an 'unconditioned, incomparable value' are problematic because value is essentially a comparative estimation and cannot coherently be absolute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require accounts of dignity/value that explain reference points and comparisons. Anti-pattern: using rhetorical grandeur ('dignity') to paper over conceptual gaps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral theory should include moral considerability beyond rational beings
rubrics_metrics.description: The exclusion of animals from direct moral duties (treating them merely as means) is morally objectionable; a sound ethics should recognise moral significance in living beings beyond narrowly defined rational agents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a theory's scope arbitrarily restricts moral regard (e.g., because of cultural or theological inheritance). Example: Kant's position that duties to animals are only duties to oneself is criticized as enabling cruelty; a better theory accounts for sympathy and intrinsic value in other sentient beings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for motive and interest—actions are not motive-less
rubrics_metrics.description: Assertions that moral action can renounce all interest (i.e., that the will can act without any motive) are incoherent; motives/interests are the causes of volition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A moral account should acknowledge that actions are motivated and explain how motives can ground duty without requiring the impossible notion of motive-less volition. Anti-pattern: treating 'duty without interest' as a real psychological possibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles should be practicable and not rest on utopian abstractions
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructs like a 'Kingdom of Ends' composed of pure rational beings who will only will autonomy are utopian abstractions; moral principles should be practicable and intelligible in real human contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the principle presumes an unrealizable transformation of human psychology or social conditions. If a principle only works in an abstract utopia, its applicability as a moral foundation is limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical ethics should avoid vacuous slogans and provide substantive grounding
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases such as 'human dignity' may serve as comforting slogans but are inadequate unless given clear, substantive grounding and explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require that central moral claims be backed by coherent arguments, not merely rhetorical elevation. Test by asking what the slogan adds conceptually and whether it resolves real ethical disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics' true substance should be simple, actionable: 'Do no harm; help where possible'
rubrics_metrics.description: The author proposes the simplest workable moral foundation: 'Neminem laede, immo omnes, quantum potes, juva' — do no one harm and help everyone as far as you can.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer moral formulations that yield clear, actionable demands and can serve as practical guidance. Use this as a touchstone to judge more abstruse formulations: do they reduce to or support this simple injunction?

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral psychology—sympathy (treating others as ends) is the basis of character
rubrics_metrics.description: A subject's disposition to treat others as ends rather than merely as means (capacity for sympathy) is the criterion of ethical character and the psychological basis for morality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate moral agents and systems by their promotion or suppression of sympathetic attitudes. Example: practical tests include whether, in ordinary interactions, agents see others as potential means only (egoism) or also as ends (sympathy).
